children: For over a decade, India’s renewable energy litigation revolved around tariffs — adoption of rates discovered through bidding and attempts by distribution licensees (discoms) to reopen concluded power purchase agreements (PPAs). Today, the disputes reaching the electricity regulatory commissions (ERCs), the Appellate Tribunal for Electricity (APTEL) and the Supreme Court are related to risk across the project life, including changes in law, curtailment, payment security, and land and habitat constraints. The question is whether a framework built to determine tariffs can coherently adjudicate the risk.

Under the Electricity Act, 2003, Section 61(h) directs commissions to promote renewable generation when framing tariff terms, Section 62 governs determined tariffs, and Section 63 mandates the adoption of tariffs discovered through transparent bidding. Section 86(1)(e) requires State commissions to promote renewable generation and specify purchase obligations, while Section 86(1)(f) vests them with the adjudication of disputes between licensees and generators, including reference to arbitration.

Following the Gujarat Urja Vikas Nigam Ltd vs Essar Power Ltd case (2008), the Delhi High Court in the Enerica Infra Pvt Ltd vs NTPC Vidyut Vyapar Nigam Ltd case in October this year held that PPA arbitration clauses yield to this provision and dismissed a Section (Arbitration Act) petition against encashment of bank guarantee. Risk allocation, by contrast, rests on subordinate instruments like the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy’s bidding guidelines, with standard change-in-law and termination clauses, and the Ministry of Power’s Must-Run Rules, 2021, Change in Law Rules, 2021, and Late Payment Surcharge Rules, 2022. A tariff statute now carries life-of-project disputes.

Discoms urge a stricter reading of the change-in-law clauses. In the Energy Watchdog vs CERC case (2017), the Supreme Court insisted on fidelity to contractual text but confirmed that genuine changes in law trigger relief.

Developers have secured relief qua safeguard duty and GST, and in the Uttar Haryana Bijli Vitran Nigam Ltd vs Adani Power Ltd case (2023), the Supreme Court upheld carrying cost on restitutionary principles.
Therefore, the contest has now shifted to quantification and interest.

In the National Solar Energy Federation of India vs Tamil Nadu Electricity Regulatory Commission case (August 2021), APTEL held that the must-run status is binding, that backing down on commercial grounds is impermissible, and compensation is payable. Discoms and load despatch centres continue to invoke the grid security exception preserved by the Must Run Rules, so the contest is now evidentiary: Whether despatch logs disclose a security constraint?

The newest front is environmental. In the MK Ranjitsinh vs Union of India case, the Supreme Court’s 2021 directions to place transmission lines underground in the Great Indian Bustard’s habitat stalled projects in Rajasthan and Gujarat. Its March 2024 judgment recalibrated the directions through an expert committee and recognised a right against the adverse effects of climate change under Articles 14 and 21. Developers now claim the resulting costs and delays as change in law or force majeure, claims that remain contested.

On each front, the framework is sound in principle but weak in execution. Three major reforms are overdue. Change-in-law compensation should be computed by formula and adjusted automatically under the Change in Law Rules. Load despatch centres should publish auditable despatch data, placing the burden of justifying curtailment on the curtailing entity. Forest, wildlife and land clearances need a time-bound, single-window process aligned with bid timelines. Until then, these disputes will grow more evidentiary, technical and protracted.

A tariff framework can adjudicate life-of-project risk, but only if the risk is governed by data and deadlines rather than discretion. Formulas, transparent despatch records and predictable clearances would let ERCs and APTEL decide these disputes on facts, not competing narratives. Predictability should be priced into every bid — India’s renewable capacity targets depend on it.

title: The emerging new dispute landscape in India’s renewable energy sector
